item.title: Trump announces at a Georgia campaign rally that Audi will build a new auto factory in the state
item.description: President Donald Trump on Saturday announced that Audi will build an automobile plant in Georgia as he tries to deliver on his promise to bolster American manufacturing in the final days before the ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: PERRY, Ga. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Saturday announced that Audi will build an automobile plant in Georgia as he tries to deliver on his promise to bolster American manufacturing in the final days before the midterm elections. Speaking at a campaign rally in Perry, Georgia, where he sought to boost Republican candidates, Trump said Audi — the German luxury brand owned by Volkswagen — would commit US$4.2 billion in nearby Macon to begin construction on a plant that will produce 200,000 cars a year. “Think of that. 200,000 cars a year. That’s incredible,” Trump said, crediting his aggressive and unpopular tariff policies for the company’s decision to build the plant. The announcement seemed timed to offer a last-minute boost to Republican candidates in the battleground state, including Rep. Mike Collins, who is trying to unseat Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. Trump has spent October campaigning in reliably Republican states as the party tries to hold onto its majorities in the House and Senate. Trump won Georgia in 2024 after losing it in 2020. Trump was joined on stage by Gernot Döllner, the chairman of the board of management at Audi, who said the plant would be producing “our biggest and most premium SUVs.” “This is a long-term investment, because we believe in the American market,” he said. Audi, in a news release, said the plant — its first in Georgia — would create approximately 4,500 jobs and that construction was scheduled to begin in 2027, with production beginning in the early 2030s. Republicans are bracing for losses in the Nov. 3 midterm elections as they contend with an unpopular president and an electorate that is angry over high costs and the ongoing war in Iran. At the rally, Rick Jackson, the Republican candidate for Georgia governor, thanked Trump for the plans. “Thank you on behalf of Georgia for putting the biggest economic deal in Georgia history right here today,” he said. ___ Colvin reported from New York. Jill Colvin And Josh Boak, The Associated Press

item.title: S&P/TSX composite down more than 150 points as oil tops US$100 per barrel
item.description: Canada’s main stock index was down more than 150 points, despite strength in the energy sector as the price of oil rose to top US$100 per barrel.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index finished the week in negative territory as North American markets felt pressure from higher oil prices and concerns about the AI trade. “The main setbacks for the markets, TSX and North America in general, came really in two forms,” said Allan Small, senior investment adviser at iA Private Wealth.  “One is this idea of a technology pullback ... and this idea that perhaps companies are spending too much on AI and not getting the return on their investment for the capital that they are putting out, and that is a big fear.”  The S&P/TSX composite index was down 185.27 points at 35,788.18.     In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 652.82 points at 52,215.16. The S&P 500 index was down 39.75 points at 7,623.68, while the Nasdaq composite was down 53.52 points at 25,955.34. Small said another risk facing the tech sector is that “AI can’t just go to the moon forever.” “At some point, memory chips, the production of them would have to slow because the market would have enough memory chips.” But falling AI stock prices could also mark a buying opportunity for some investors.  “There are a lot of names that are a lot cheaper than they were just a little while ago, although I will say that for tech, the highs were probably back at the beginning of the summer,” Small said.  He said the second major issue that markets grappled with this week was higher energy prices from the war in the Middle East and fears of potential escalation.  “We’re seeing oil prices move higher on this idea ... that after the U.S. midterms, the war could ramp up once again. We have not seen really any missiles flying for a while now, but President Trump made some comments recently which has led people to believe that there could be renewed hostilities in the Middle East,” he said.  The December crude oil contract was up US$3.80 at US$103.27 per barrel. Higher energy prices are also playing a crucial role in investor expectations that the Bank of Canada will hike its key lending rate next week. Financial market odds for a hike next Wednesday stood at nearly 78 per cent as of Friday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.     “My view on that is I think it would be foolish for the Bank of Canada to hike interest rates. I think it would be foolish for the Bank of Canada to focus on inflation when we have an economy that is really not doing a heck of a lot,” Small said, adding that growth has been muted.  The U.S. Federal Reserve is also scheduled to make an interest rate announcement on Wednesday.  “The odds of a hike in the U.S. are down quite substantially ... so it doesn’t look like they’re going to go. The odds are now that if they move, they’ll move in December,” Small said.  The Canadian dollar traded for 71.46 cents US compared with 71.32 cents US on Thursday.   The December gold contract was down US$52.50 at US$4,007.90 an ounce. --- Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

item.title: Wall Street mostly loses ground under pressure from rising oil prices
item.description: Futures are lower as oil prices reach levels not seen since May amid halting efforts to bring the U.S. and Iran back to the negotiation table.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Stocks on Wall Street closed broadly lower Friday as oil prices climbed to their highest level in more than four years, ratcheting up pressure on the market. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent, adding to its decline from a day before. The index posted its second-straight weekly loss. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after giving up a modest gain. Rising oil prices weighed heavily on the market, where nearly three out of every four stocks within the benchmark S&P 500 index fell. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 3.1 per cent to settle at US$116.72. It has surged from less than US$97 at the start of October and is now at its highest level since June 2022. Several AI-related companies rallied, helping ease some of the impact from the broader market slide. Micron Technology rose 2.5 per cent, Intel gained 1.7 per cent, Microsoft added 0.7 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices closed 1.7 per cent higher. The tech sector’s influence is also capable of quickly switching over to a heavy weight. Stocks that have benefited from the frenzy over AI have been swinging over rising worries about their path ahead. Investors are worried about whether their high prices are justified. Many of those companies have been borrowing to fund investments in AI technology and high interest rates are making those loans more expensive. “Investors appear increasingly focused on the economics of AI, particularly the substantial upfront costs required to build AI infrastructure and the uncertainty around the timing of returns on those investments,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, in a research note. The latest round of corporate earnings are being closely watched to help get a better sense of whether those investments are paying off, or might pay off. Several influential AI-related companies report their latest financial results next week, including Google’s parent, Alphabet, along with Microsoft and Amazon. Industrial companies had some of the biggest losses. Caterpillar fell 2.4 per cent. American Express slumped 3.7 per cent, one of several financial stocks that lost ground, despite r eporting profits for its most recent quarter that beat analysts’ forecasts. The company did announce its first major job cuts in roughly a decade. JPMorgan Chase fell 1.5 per cent, Citigroup dropped 1.5 per cent and Capital One Financial slid 1 per cent. While higher oil prices weighed down much of the market, they helped boost energy companies. Chevron rose 2.9 per cent and ConocoPhillips gained 3.6 per cent. European markets closed mostly lower. France’s main index fell 0.4 per cent, though yields on French government bonds eased a bit. Treasury yields in the U.S. edged higher following sharp drops on Thursday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.99 per cent from 4.96 per cent late Thursday. Yields have been rising globally, partly over worries about governments taking on too much debt. Inflation also remains a concern and is stubbornly well above 3 per cent in the U.S. That prompted the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate at its last meeting in an effort to cool inflation. Wall Street expects the central bank to hold rates steady at its meeting next week, but is leaning heavily toward another rate hike in December. Wall Street will also get several big economic updates next week, including the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. The personal consumption expenditures index, or PCE, is expected to show that inflation rose at a 3.7 per cent rate in September, sharply above the Fed’s 2 per cent target. The U.S. war with Iran has severely cut the world’s oil supply, driving energy prices higher and fueling a sharp jump in the cost of everything from gasoline to food and clothes. All told, the S&P 500 fell 39.75 points to 7,623.68. The Dow dropped 652.82 points to 52,215.16, and the Nasdaq gave up 53.52 points to close at 25,955.34. --- Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press

item.title: Rogers seeks to offset hit from CRTC fee ban as wireless service revenue dips in Q3
item.description: Rogers Communications Inc. says it is seeking to offset the hit it has taken from the CRTC’s recent ban on telecommunications carriers charging certain administrative fees.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Rogers Communications Inc. says it is seeking to offset the hit it has taken from the CRTC’s recent ban on telecommunications carriers charging certain administrative fees. While Rogers reported a year-over-year increase in overall revenue during its most recent quarter, primarily due to growth in its media division, the company said wireless service revenue decreased one per cent. During its third quarter, Rogers’ mobile phone average monthly revenue per user was $55.22, down from $56.70 in the same quarter of the prior year. Chief financial officer Glenn Brandt said the “largest impact” to that closely watched figure came from the CRTC’s move in June to prohibit telecoms from charging customers when they activate, change or cancel plans. “The purpose of those setup fees was exactly that — to offset costs of account changes or new accounts coming on,” Brandt told analysts on a conference call Friday. “The charge disappeared (due to) the CRTC decision. The costs don’t.” He said Rogers put in place some “early initiatives” during the quarter to recover some of those costs, but “there’s still more work to do.” “We’re now moving back to finding alternatives for covering those costs, shipping costs, for example … so that effort remains ongoing.” The CRTC has said the new rules are meant to make it easier for customers to switch internet and cellphone plans without having to worry about unexpected charges. The regulator is in the midst of a review into whether Rogers, along with rivals Bell Canada and Telus Corp., violated the ban by introducing new fees around the time it took effect. It said Rogers began charging customers a $40 device setup fee, $25 shipping charge, and an unspecified SIM card fee in mid-June that “would not appear” to qualify for an exemption under the rules for optional services or products that consumers consent to purchase. Rogers has argued the device setup fee is related to an optional purchase. It also said the shipping and SIM fees were not new, and that the latter is only charged when a customer replaces a lost or damaged SIM, rather than at activation. Overall, the quarter saw a “less active telecom market,” said Rogers president and CEO Tony Staffieri said, as the company reported a profit attributable to shareholders of $482 million. “In wireless, we stayed focused on financials versus chasing subscriber volume in what is typically a busy back-to-school quarter,” he told analysts. The company reported 17,000 total mobile phone net subscriber additions, including 6,000 postpaid — those who pay a monthly bill for their wireless services after charges have accumulated. That was down from 62,000 postpaid additions in the same quarter last year. Rogers’ monthly churn — a measure of those who cancelled their service — for net postpaid mobile subscribers was 1.03 per cent, up from 0.99 per cent during its previous third quarter. Retail internet net additions totalled 10,000, down from 29,000 a year earlier. The company said its profit amounted to 88 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30. The result compared with a profit of $5.71 billion or $10.54 per diluted share a year ago when it saw a $5-billion non-cash gain related to its stake in Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment and $151-million gain on the redemption of long-term debt. On an adjusted basis, Rogers said it earned $704 million in net income, or $1.29 per diluted share in its latest quarter, down from an adjusted profit of $1.37 per diluted share a year ago. Revenue totalled $5.44 billion, up from $5.35 billion in the same quarter last year. “Financial results were in line with our forecast while subscriber growth was a little lighter than our forecast,” said RBC analyst Drew McReynolds in a note. “We view the results as largely neutral for the shares at current levels.” Earlier this month, Rogers completed its $4.35-billion purchase of the remaining 25 per cent stake in MLSE it did not already hold, giving it complete ownership of the sports conglomerate that includes the Maple Leafs, Raptors, Toronto FC and Argonauts. Staffieri reiterated Rogers’ plan to sell a minority interest in its consolidated sports, media and entertainment portfolio to third-party investors, adding he remains “bullish about our plan to unlock shareholder value and drive long-term growth.” Rogers is targeting the first half of 2027 to close that minority interest sale. “Investor interest in these assets is substantial as sports franchise valuations continue to rise,” Staffieri said. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026. By Sammy Hudes BNN Bloomberg, CTV News and CP24 are owned by Bell Media, which is a division of BCE.
